analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal taxes on capital gains, interest, and dividends and cuts taxes on Social Security benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2003, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop taxing capital gains for individuals and stop taxing interest and dividend income entirely, while rolling back the 1993 rule that taxes up to 85% of Social Security benefits for higher-income retirees. Because most capital gains, dividends, and interest go to the wealthiest households, the bulk of the tax cut would flow to them. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with capital gains, dividend, and interest income — which are concentrated among the wealthiest Americans — would pay no federal tax on that income at all. Retirees whose combined income exceeds $25,000 ($32,000 for couples) would see their Social Security benefit taxation capped at the pre-1993 50% level instead of 85% [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Excludes all net capital gains from gross income for taxpayers other than corporations, effective for tax years beginning after 2002 [S3][S2].

Excludes all interest and dividend income received by individuals from gross income, with carve-outs for certain farmer cooperative dividends, mutual fund and REIT capital-gain distributions, and ESOP dividends [S2][S3].

Repeals the 1993 change that taxes up to 85% of Social Security and Railroad Retirement benefits, restoring the prior 50% cap, and replaces the lost Medicare (Hospital Insurance) trust fund revenue with transfers from the general fund [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would lose all revenue currently collected on individual capital gains, dividends, and interest. That revenue loss would either show up as larger deficits or require other taxes or spending cuts to offset. The general fund would also cover the revenue the Medicare trust fund loses from the Social Security benefit change [S3]. Because investment income is concentrated at the top, the tax burden shifted away from wealthy households would fall proportionally on everyone else.

drawbacks.text: The investment-income exclusion would eliminate the entire federal tax on the income forms most heavily held by the wealthiest households, while wage earners' paychecks would remain fully taxed — the largest share of the revenue loss goes to those at the top [S2][S3].

The bill has no offsetting revenue; the Social Security benefit change alone requires ongoing general-fund appropriations to backfill the Medicare trust fund, meaning the provisions add to the deficit or force other program cuts [S3].

Excluding interest from income invites tax sheltering — the bill itself includes anti-abuse coordination rules limiting the exclusion for borrowed funds used to buy tax-exempt assets, an acknowledgment that the provision would otherwise reward borrowing to avoid tax [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The Social Security benefit provision is a genuine, targeted benefit for middle-income retirees. But the core of the bill — a total exemption for capital gains, interest, and dividends — is far larger and overwhelmingly flows to the wealthiest households, with no funding source. The cost to the Treasury and to wage earners who keep paying tax on their income would substantially outweigh the narrow senior benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee after referral in April 2003 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Beauprez introduced the bill on April 11, 2003, with seven Republican cosponsors [S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the largest investment-income tax cut never took effect; general taxpayers and federal programs were spared the revenue loss, while wealthy investors forgo a full exemption and higher-income retirees continue to have up to 85% of benefits taxed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; wealthy investors lose a windfall

for.name: Rep. Bob Beauprez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven Republican cosponsors

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were House Republicans and no Democrat supported it, but no vote was ever held, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would exempt capital gains, interest, and dividends entirely — income forms concentrated at the top of the income scale — while wage income stays taxed. Their gain would be paid for through deficits or by other taxpayers.
Eliminating tax on investment returns would raise the appeal of financial assets and increase flows through brokerages, banks, and funds, at a cost to Treasury revenue that others must cover.

industries.industry: Social Security and Railroad Retirement beneficiaries
industries.note: Higher-income retirees would keep more of their benefits, with the shortfall backfilled from the general fund rather than the trust funds themselves.
